title: s-Block Elements
tagline: The Group 1 alkali metals and Group 2 alkaline earth metals: their electronic configuration, trends in physical and chemical properties, important compounds, and the diagonal relationship.

overview.intro: The s-block elements are a good place to see periodic trends in action. Group 1 contains the alkali metals, and Group 2 contains the alkaline earth metals. Both groups are reactive, and both become more reactive in some ways as you go down the group. They form colorless compounds in many cases, they react with water and oxygen in characteristic ways, and their chemistry helps explain why the periodic table is so useful. This chapter looks at the general features first and then at some important compounds and the diagonal relationship between lithium and magnesium.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Electronic configuration of Groups 1 and 2; atomic and ionic sizes; ionization enthalpy; reactivity with water and air; oxides and hydroxides; salts such as sodium chloride, sodium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide and gypsum; diagonal relationship

learningOutcomes: Describe the general electronic configuration of s-block elements.
Explain trends in size and ionization enthalpy in Groups 1 and 2.
Describe the reactivity of these elements with oxygen and water.
Compare the chemistry of Group 1 and Group 2 elements.
Describe important compounds of sodium and calcium.
Explain the diagonal relationship between lithium and magnesium.
Remember that s-block elements are not all equally reactive.
Avoid overgeneralizing from one member of a group to the whole group.

blocks.text: The s-block elements are those in which the outermost electron enters an s orbital. Group 1 elements have an outer configuration of ns1, and Group 2 elements have ns2. This simple difference has big consequences. Group 1 metals have one electron to lose and form +1 ions easily. Group 2 metals form +2 ions. Both groups are metals, and both are electropositive, but Group 1 metals are generally more reactive than the corresponding Group 2 metals in many common reactions.

items: Group 1: outer configuration ns1, forms +1 ions.
Group 2: outer configuration ns2, forms +2 ions.
Both groups are electropositive metals.
Group 1 metals are generally more reactive in many common reactions.
The s-block gives a clear picture of group trends.

items.text: Sodium forms Na+ by losing one electron. Magnesium forms Mg2+ by losing two electrons. The difference in charge affects many properties, including the character of their compounds.
items.note: The example links electronic configuration directly to ionic charge.

learn.title: Trends in size and ionization enthalpy

blocks.text: As you go down either group, the atoms get larger because more electron shells are added. Larger atoms usually have lower ionization enthalpy, so it becomes easier to remove the outermost electron. This helps explain why reactivity increases down Group 1 for many reactions. In Group 2, similar trends appear, although the chemistry is more nuanced because two electrons are involved. The important skill is to connect the trend in size with the trend in ionization enthalpy and then with reactivity.

items: Atomic size increases down the group.
Ionization enthalpy generally decreases down the group.
Lower ionization enthalpy often means greater reactivity.
Trends are consistent but not identical in every reaction.
Size and ionization enthalpy are closely linked.

items.text: In Group 1, cesium is larger and has a lower ionization enthalpy than lithium, which is one reason why cesium is more reactive in many situations. The trend helps explain the group behavior.
items.note: The example shows how atomic properties explain a familiar group trend.

blocks.text: Alkali metals react with water to produce hydroxides and hydrogen, and the reaction becomes more vigorous down the group for many members. They also react with oxygen, forming oxides, peroxides or superoxides depending on the metal. Alkaline earth metals also react with water and oxygen, but often less violently than alkali metals in comparable situations. These reactions are a classic illustration of how group position relates to chemical behavior, and they show that reactivity is not just a label but something that can be predicted from electronic structure and trends.

items: Alkali metals react with water to give hydroxides and hydrogen.
Reactivity with water often increases down Group 1.
Alkali metals can form oxides, peroxides and superoxides.
Alkaline earth metals also react, but often less violently.
Reaction products depend on the metal and conditions.

items.text: Sodium reacts with water more vigorously than many other metals, and the reaction produces hydrogen. The heat produced can even ignite the hydrogen in some cases.
items.note: The example shows why alkali metals must be handled with care.

blocks.text: Sodium compounds are extremely important in everyday life and in industry. Sodium chloride is common salt. Sodium carbonate is used in glassmaking and in many industrial processes. Sodium bicarbonate is used as a mild base and in baking. These compounds are not just laboratory curiosities; they are familiar and useful. Their chemistry is also a good way to practice thinking about acid-base behavior and thermal decomposition, because some of these salts decompose on heating in characteristic ways.

items: Sodium chloride is common salt.
Sodium carbonate is used in glass and industry.
Sodium bicarbonate is a mild base and is used in baking.
Important sodium compounds are both common and industrially useful.
Many of these compounds decompose on heating in characteristic ways.

items.text: Sodium bicarbonate can decompose on heating to give sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. This is one reason it is useful in baking, because the carbon dioxide helps dough rise.
items.note: The example connects a chemical reaction to a familiar household use.

blocks.text: Calcium compounds are also important. Calcium oxide, or quicklime, reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, or slaked lime, which is used in construction and in water treatment. Gypsum and plaster of Paris are calcium-based materials used in building and in models. Another familiar example is calcium carbonate, found in limestone and marble. These compounds show that the chemistry of calcium is not esoteric; it appears in materials people use every day.

items: Calcium oxide is quicklime.
Calcium hydroxide is slaked lime.
Gypsum and plaster of Paris are calcium sulfate materials.
Calcium carbonate is found in limestone and marble.
Calcium compounds are widely used in building and industry.

items.text: When water is added to calcium oxide, a vigorous reaction forms calcium hydroxide and releases heat. This process, slaking of lime, is a good example of a familiar industrial reaction.
items.note: The example links a simple reaction to a well-known building material process.

blocks.text: Sometimes an element in one group resembles the element diagonally below it in the next group. The most famous example is the diagonal relationship between lithium and magnesium. Their compounds show similarities that are not seen as clearly between lithium and other alkali metals. This happens because the two elements have similar charge density and related chemical behavior. The diagonal relationship is a useful reminder that chemical similarity does not follow only vertical groups.

items: Diagonal relationship means similarity between diagonally related elements.
Lithium and magnesium show such a relationship.
It arises from similar charge density and related properties.
It shows similarity is not always vertical.
It is a good test of understanding periodic trends.

items.text: Lithium and magnesium can form nitrides more readily than other alkali metals do, and their carbonates decompose differently from those of some other Group 1 metals. These similarities stand out when you compare lithium with magnesium instead of with sodium.
items.note: The example makes the diagonal relationship concrete.

blocks.text: One common mistake is to think that all alkali metals behave exactly the same. They do not; the trend is important but it is not identical in every detail. Another mistake is to assume that Group 2 elements are just weaker versions of Group 1 elements. They have their own chemistry, including the +2 oxidation state and different compound behavior. A third mistake is to forget that reactivity trends can depend on the reaction being considered. The best habit is to use trends as a guide, not as a substitute for specifics.

items: Alkali metals are not all identical in detail.
Group 2 elements have their own chemistry.
Reactivity trends can vary with the reaction.
Diagonal relationships exist and are important.
Use trends as guidance, not as absolute rules.

items.text: If a student says lithium is chemically identical to sodium in every respect, that is inaccurate. The diagonal relationship shows that lithium has special similarities with magnesium, which would not be predicted if group membership alone told the whole story.
items.note: The example stresses the value of exceptions and relationships in the s-block.
